name: Lena Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Lena, and thank you for this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Nothing you say will be tied to your name. Can you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on nights at Brandt Metalworks, on the stamping line. We press steel strip into hinges and brackets for kitchen cupboards. I feed the coil, set the die, which is the shaped steel block that cuts and bends the part, watch the presses thump away, and pull samples every half hour to measure. Seven years there now. I like nights, it's quieter and the supervisors leave you alone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm. Bang, bang, bang, and you can tell from the sound if a die is about to crack. The pay is good, and with the night premium it's better. What wears me out is sleeping in the day in summer, and my left shoulder from lifting die sets. I live on my own in my grandmother's old flat, which she left me, so no rent, which is a blessing. I don't touch the AI stuff on phones. Never saw the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was hype like a lot of things. I'm not someone who posts online. At work I'd shrug and say, see, presses still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me, which suits me. I'd still be on nights, still on the same line. I like my life the way it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working nights, keep saving. I put about half my pay away because I've got no rent. Maybe finally get my shoulder looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't see the point of AI. Would anything at Brandt change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office uses it to plan the coil orders, I wouldn't notice. The presses already have sensors that stop them when something's wrong. That's been there since before I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about work, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My shoulder, mostly. A lot of the older press operators have bad shoulders or bad hearing by fifty. I'd like to do this job another twenty years without wrecking my shoulder.

say: It was **hype**, like a lot of things.
At work I'd shrug and say **presses** still need people.
think: Nothing changes for me, which **suits me** fine.
I'd still be on **nights** on the same stamping line.
do: Keep saving about **half my pay**, since I have no rent.
S0.quote: I'd like to do this job another twenty years without wrecking my shoulder.
fieldNote: Owning her flat **rent-free** gives her an unusually large cushion.
Her real worry is **physical wear**, shoulders and hearing, not technology.
She prefers **routine** and quiet nights and wants nothing to change.

steps.text: Keep working nights on the stamping line at Brandt
Book a doctor's appointment for the sore left shoulder

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible for companies to use it where it makes sense, as long as they're decent about the people. I wouldn't make speeches. I'd say that if someone asked me at the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be watching the presses. We've already got a transfer robot moving parts between press two and three on day shift. If more of those come, they need fewer of us on a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much the first year. Keep saving, maybe a bit more. I'm not doing courses or downloading apps. I'd wait and see what Brandt actually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when they say a storm might come but the sky's still clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Brandt took one operator off each line, I'd go to an older press shop that hasn't bought robots yet. There are four or five stamping and press shops within a short drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brandt would you think of first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gosia in the office does the orders and invoices, and she's been there twenty years. That's the kind of job the card means. I'd feel bad for her, but there's nothing I can do about it.

say: Companies should use it where it **makes sense**, if they treat people decently.
I'd only say so if someone **asked** at the canteen.
think: A **transfer robot** already moves parts between presses on day shift.
More of those means **fewer operators** per line.
do: Move to an **older press shop** if Brandt cuts an operator per line.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a storm forecast under a clear sky.
S1.quote: If Brandt took one operator off each line, I'd go to an older press shop that hasn't bought robots yet.
fieldNote: Her escape plan is to find an **older, less automated** shop, not to learn new skills.
She already sees the **transfer robot** as the first sign on her own line.
She feels for office colleagues but stays **detached**, not political.

steps.text: Put a little more of each paycheque into savings
Watch whether Brandt cuts an operator from each press line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and someone should have slowed it down. Not banning it, just making companies go at a pace people can handle. Online I'd say nothing, I'm not on there much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out by 2031. Presses are the easiest thing in the world for a robot to feed. Every shop in the area would buy them at once, so my plan of going somewhere older wouldn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare coin away for three years and stop buying things I don't need. I'd rent my spare room to a student for extra money. And I'd find out what support the government gives people who lose their jobs to this, before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep coming back to the shoulder, and thinking I'll have wrecked it for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rent the spare room. Is that a big step for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very big. I like my own space, I've never shared since my grandmother died. But a lodger's money every month is safer than hoping. My cousin Agata did it and says it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2031, when the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I can't picture it. Maybe a shop, or cleaning, something people still want a person for. I'd have the flat and some savings, so I wouldn't starve, but I'd be lost.

say: It's **too fast**, and someone should have slowed it down.
Companies should go at a **pace** people can handle, not ban it.
think: Presses are the **easiest thing** for a robot to feed.
Every shop nearby would **automate at once**, so switching shops won't help.
do: Stop buying **anything unneeded** for three years.
Rent the **spare room** to a student.
Find out what **government support** exists before I need it.
feel: **Frightened**, and bitter about a damaged **shoulder** for nothing.
S2.quote: Presses are the easiest thing in the world for a robot to feed.
fieldNote: Her fallback of moving to an **older shop** collapses here.
Renting the spare room is a **big personal step** for someone who values solitude.
The **owned flat** keeps her from panic, but she has no picture of what's next.

steps.text: Stop buying anything unneeded for three years
Rent the spare room to a student
Ask the job centre what support exists for laid-off workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, too fast, but at least it gives people warning. I'd say companies should have to tell staff years ahead. That's only fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots on the presses around 2034 means about eight more years for me. I'd be thirty-five. Enough to save a lot more, not enough to stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving hard and rent the spare room from next year, not straight away. I'd keep my head down at Brandt and wait to see how quickly the robots actually spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slower. Like a toothache you keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about learning something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something hands-on that a robot would find hard. People talk about care work. I don't know if I could do it, but I'd think about it around 2032, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Agata about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm saving like mad and keeping my options open. She'd tell me to do a course. She always does.

say: It's still too fast, but at least there's **warning**.
Companies should have to **tell staff** years ahead.
Giving that notice is **only fair** to workers.
think: Robots on the presses around **2034** gives me about eight more years.
That's enough to **save more**, not enough to stop worrying.
do: Rent the **spare room** from next year.
Wait and see how quickly **robots spread** before deciding anything.
feel: **Anxious**, but slower, like a toothache kept at bay.
S3.quote: Robots on the presses around 2034 means about eight more years for me.
fieldNote: She uses the time to **build savings**, not to change course.
**Care work** surfaces as a vague idea, deferred to 2032.
Her cousin is the **nudge** toward courses she keeps resisting.

steps.text: Keep saving half of each paycheque
Rent the spare room to a lodger from next year
Hold off on any course until around 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a reasonable amount of time, and people shouldn't panic. Companies and the government have time to plan. I'd say that and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a long way off. Robots on the presses around 2039, I'd be forty. Ten years ago I was seventeen and I didn't know what a die set was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working nights, keep saving, see the doctor about my shoulder. I'd think about it properly in 2033 or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a bit. It's far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you do anything differently this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Not this year. I don't change things for something that might happen in thirteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 2039 is far. Is there a part of you that worries anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Forty is late to start something new, and I know I'm not good with change. But I'd have the flat paid and a lot saved by then, so I'd manage.

say: Ten years is a **reasonable** amount of time, so people shouldn't panic.
Companies and the **government** have time to plan.
think: Robots on the presses around **2039** means I'd be forty.
That's as far ahead as **seventeen** is behind me.
do: Keep working **nights** and saving as now.
Think about the future properly around **2033**.
feel: Mildly **uneasy**, because it feels far away.
S4.quote: Ten years ago I was seventeen and I didn't know what a die set was.
fieldNote: Distance makes it **abstract** for her; she won't act this year.
She admits she's **not good with change** and that forty is late to restart.
The **paid-off flat** is her quiet confidence in every scenario.

steps.text: Carry on with nights on the Brandt stamping line
Revisit plans for the future around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years, and every press shop goes at once. What would help is proper notice from companies, years not weeks, and some money to live on while you find something else. I don't need fancy courses, just time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the people who don't want to change. Everyone talks like we should all become programmers. Some of us just want to do a good job on a press, go home and sleep.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks like we should all become programmers. Some of us just want to do a good job on a press, go home and sleep.
portrait: Lena, 27, runs a **stamping press** line on nights, making hinges and brackets.
She lives alone in an **inherited flat** with no rent, so she saves half her pay.
She avoids AI tools and new tech, and her instinct is to **wait and see**.
She's calm or uneasy in slow worlds and **alarmed** by AGI in 2028.
Her fallbacks are a **lodger**, savings and government support, not retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because every press shop nearby would automate at once.
whatWouldHelp: Years of **notice** from companies before robots arrive.
Some **money to live on** while finding other work.
